recommendations:
VOICE SAMPLE: this answers the user's offer to record now. Record 2 takes of the script in the next item and upload the cleaner one (about 80-100 s of speech).
- Room: quiet, with soft furnishings (a closet full of clothes works).
- Mic: phone or USB mic 15-20 cm from the mouth, slightly off-axis.
- Off: fans, AC and phone notifications. No music, reverb or noise-reduction plugins.
- Levels: peaks around -6 to -3 dBFS, average near -20 dB RMS (ElevenLabs asks for -23 to -18 dB RMS with a -3 dB true peak).
- File: WAV, or MP3 at 192 kbps or higher.
- Delivery: your exact reel voice, brisk and forward at about 165-180 wpm, with the same energy start to finish. No whispers, laughs or character voices, because the clone copies the performance.
- Trim any silence longer than about 1 s.
Then create the Instant Voice Clone in ElevenLabs, or record it with Higgsfield's Create Voice widget if narration will be generated with Eleven v4 on Higgsfield. Expect a consent check.

SCRIPT TO READ (original, 230 words, 1,309 characters, about 80-95 s; it avoids the reference creator's lines):

Here's something nobody tells you about launch night. The moment a giant game goes live, millions of people press the same button within the same few minutes. And somewhere, a wall of servers has to say yes to every single one of them.

Think about that. One button. Millions of thumbs. Zero second chances.

So how do you get ready for a wave like that? You rehearse it. Engineers simulate the rush over and over, until the machines stop flinching. They add capacity. They plan for things to break. They watch the dashboards go red, then amber, then green.

Now, some numbers. One. Ten. A hundred. A thousand. Ten thousand. A million. Fifty million. A billion. Past a certain point, your brain just files every number under 'a lot'. And that's exactly why this stuff is fascinating.

Here's what happens behind the curtain. Behind every loading screen, there's a team that hasn't slept properly in a week. Behind every smooth first mission, there's a fix you will never notice.

Quick question. When you finally get in, are you rushing the story? Or are you just driving around at sunset with the radio up?

Be honest.

Because either way, the city doesn't care how fast you are. It's been waiting for you for years. And in a few days, the lights come on.

That's the view from backstage. Same time tomorrow.

VOICE MODEL AND SETTINGS:
- A/B test: run one 60-word paragraph containing numbers through the same clone on Eleven v4 and on Multilingual v2. Keep whichever holds timbre and diction better at speed.
- Starting points (to tune by ear): v4 stability 0.45-0.55, similarity 0.80. v2 stability 0.45, similarity 0.80, style 0, speaker boost on, speed 1.05-1.10.
- Generate 1-3 sentences per request (under about 400 characters), with 3-4 variations each (Higgsfield batch_size goes up to 4).
- Splice the best takes with 60-120 ms gaps. Regenerate single lines, never the whole reel.

TTS TEXT RULES:
- Spell numbers out for the ear ('two to the power of one hundred twenty-eight'; '340 undecillion' rather than 39 digits) and keep numerals for the captions.
- No parentheses, abbreviations or symbols.
- Pace with periods and em dashes, because v4 and v3 ignore <break>.
- Use at most 1-2 audio tags per reel, e.g. [whispers] on the midpoint rehook only.

PACE:
- Target 175-190 wpm with almost no gaps until the sign-off, like the reference (first word at 0.14 s).
- Word budgets at 185 wpm: 45 s about 139 words, 60 s about 185, 75 s about 231, 90 s about 278.
- If a v4 take reads slow, use atempo=1.06 (stay at or under about 1.10) or rubberband=tempo=1.06:formant=preserved, since v4 has no speed control.
- Start narration at or before 0.2 s, with no logo sting and no fade-in from black.

EXPORT ONE MASTER for Instagram, TikTok and Shorts (verified locally with ffmpeg 6.1.1):
ffmpeg -i edit.mov -i mix.wav -map 0:v -map 1:a -vf fps=30,format=yuv420p -c:v libx264 -preset slow -crf 17 -profile:v high -level:v 4.2 -g 60 -bf 2 -color_primaries bt709 -color_trc bt709 -colorspace bt709 -c:a aac -b:a 256k -ar 48000 -ac 2 -movflags +faststart out.mp4
- Use fps=24 instead if every source clip is 24 fps (check with ffprobe -show_entries stream=r_frame_rate), so no frames are duplicated.
- Stay SDR; do not convert to HDR.
- Generate final shots at 1080p (Kling 4.0's default) rather than upscaling 720p.

LAYOUT ON 1080x1920:
- All text and key visuals inside x 65-1015, y 269-1248.
- Captions centred around y 1080-1150, at most 2 lines of about 18 characters each.
- Hook text and number cards in the upper middle (y 650-950).
- For TikTok and Shorts, also keep the right ~150 px clear below y ~1000, where the button rails sit (my estimate).
- Day badge ('DAY 4') small at the top left, inside the box (y ~300).
- Custom cover: title inside the 3:4 profile-grid crop (y 240-1680) and ideally y 450-1150, which also survives a 4:5 feed crop (y 285-1635). Both crop sizes are unverified.

CAPTIONS:
- Burn them in, and do not also enable in-app auto captions.
- Show 2-4-word phrase chunks with the spoken word highlighted in a single accent colour. Single words flashing at 3 words/s are tiring to read.
- Font: heavy sans (Inter Black or Montserrat ExtraBold), 78-90 px, white, 6-8 px black outline plus a soft shadow, no box.
- Every number gets its own numeral card (140-180 px, 150-200 ms scale-in) timed to an impact sound.
- Word timings: forced alignment on the final voice track (e.g. WhisperX), or ElevenLabs' timestamped TTS output if the chosen model returns it. Write an ASS file and burn it with -vf ass=captions.ass. Tested template: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-echo-player/53197e09-39b2-53e1-ace7-1aefc4b23039/scratchpad/prodtest/scripts/captions_test.ass

MIX RECIPE (tested; result -14.0 LUFS, -3.8 dBTP):
- Voice stem: highpass at 90 Hz, 3:1 compression, normalised to about -17 LUFS.
- Music bed: about -20 LUFS before ducking.
- Ducking: [music][voice]sidechaincompress=threshold=0.03:ratio=8:attack=15:release=400 puts the bed about 16 dB under the voice and lets it swell back in pauses. Use 0.05:6 (about 12 dB) for hype passages and 0.02:10 (about 20 dB) under dense number passages.
- Mix with amix=normalize=0.
- Master with two-pass loudnorm=I=-14:TP=-1:LRA=11, feeding pass 1's measured_* values and linear=true into pass 2.
Full script: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-echo-player/53197e09-39b2-53e1-ace7-1aefc4b23039/scratchpad/prodtest/scripts/audio_chain_test.sh

MUSIC AND SOUND DESIGN:
- Beds: generate original instrumentals with ElevenLabs Music v2.5 on Higgsfield (force_instrumental, exact duration) and reuse one motif every day as the series' sonic brand. This avoids library-music claims; still check the plan's commercial terms.
- 0.0 s: sub hit or whoosh under the first word.
- Every number card: an impact (40-60 Hz boom plus a transient).
- Midpoint rehook: a 1.5-2 s riser, then a hard cut and 150-300 ms of near-silence before the line.
- Cuts: whooshes on only about a third of them.
- Sign-off: a 2-3 s sonic logo.
- Keep SFX peaks at least 6 dB below voice peaks.
- Higgsfield's Mirelo SFX is game-pipeline only, so get SFX elsewhere (ElevenLabs Sound Effects or a licensed library; availability not re-verified).

EDIT RHYTHM AND LOOP:
- 2-3 visual changes in the first 3 s, then a change every 2-4 s: a hard cut, a 1.00 to 1.12 punch-in, a speed ramp, a number card or an overlay. Hard-cut on every new number.
- Planning math: an 80 s reel needs about 25 shots. Using 2-4 s of each 5-6 s generation, that is about 12-18 generations per reel.
- Loop: end on the same composition as frame 1 by passing the opening still as end_image (Kling 4.0, Kling 3.0, Seedance 2.5, Veo 3.1 Lite or Hailuo 2.3). Put the branded sign-off on screen in the last 1.5 s and cut straight back to the hook with no fade.
- That the loop raises replays is an estimate, not a measurement.

AI B-ROLL WORKFLOW:
1. Key frames: 9:16 stills at 2K-4K with Nano Banana 2.1 (fixed seed) or Nano Banana Pro, Seedream 5.0 Pro, Cinema Studio Image 2.5 or Soul Cinema. Lock one style suffix for the whole series.
2. Animate: Kling 4.0 at 1080p, 5-6 s, as the workhorse. Seedance 2.5 with draft=true (480p) to approve motion, then finalize via draft_job_id. Veo 3.1 (8 s, 9:16, preview variant) for 1-2 hero realism shots per reel. Cinema Studio 3.5 with color_grading hyper_neon or cold_steel and prompt_language 'en' for stylised neon.
3. Audio: turn generated audio off where possible (Kling sound 'off' also costs fewer credits) and mute it elsewhere.
4. Clean-up: deflicker, then upscale (Topaz, or Bytedance's 'aigc' preset) only the shots that make the cut.
5. Conform everything to one frame rate.
6. Never ask a model for on-screen text, logos or trademarks (GTA, Rockstar, PlayStation, Xbox). Add all text in ffmpeg, and say 'game console' or 'neon coastal city' in prompts.

PROMPT TEMPLATE (40-80 words; one subject motion plus one camera move):
'[shot size + lens] of [subject], [single motion]. Camera: [one move, speed]. Setting: [environment]. Light: [key, practicals, haze]. Look: [palette, grade, grain]. Vertical 9:16, subject in the upper-middle third.'
- For image-to-video, describe only motion, camera and atmosphere, not what is already in the still.
- Phrase positively: describe what is in frame instead of writing 'no X'.
- Prefer 5-6 s clips over 10 s ones; they drift less (a craft heuristic).
- Avoid close-up faces and hands. Machines, light and environments stay coherent.

STARTER PROMPTS:
- ENCRYPTION: 'Extreme macro of a translucent glass padlock built from thousands of tiny glowing glyphs, its layers rotating and re-locking like a combination dial. Camera: slow push-in to the keyhole. Dark void with drifting blue data dust. Cyan rim light, magenta backlight, volumetric haze. Anamorphic 50mm, shallow depth of field, fine film grain. Vertical 9:16.'
- SERVERS: 'Low-angle wide shot down an endless aisle of black server racks in a cold vault, thousands of status LEDs pulsing in waves toward camera. Camera: steady dolly forward at walking pace. Cold steel-blue overheads, green and amber LEDs, low floor fog. 24mm, deep focus, teal shadows. Vertical 9:16, vanishing point in the upper third.'
- DATA: 'Macro inside a bundle of fiber-optic strands, pulses of white and magenta light racing toward the lens. Camera: slow forward glide. 100mm macro, very shallow focus, glossy reflections, slight motion blur. Vertical 9:16.'
- MONEY: 'Slow-motion banknotes and gold coins tumbling through a single shaft of warm light in a dark room, dust glinting. Camera: locked off with a slight upward tilt. 85mm, f/1.8 bokeh, amber key on deep black, film grain. Vertical 9:16.'
- NEON CITY: 'Aerial drone glide over a rain-soaked coastal city at night, palm-lined boulevards, pink and teal neon reflecting on wet streets, a curve of red tail lights toward the ocean. Camera: slow forward flight with a gentle descending tilt. Sodium streetlights, light rain haze. Anamorphic, teal-magenta grade, soft halation. Vertical 9:16, horizon in the upper quarter.'
- VAULT (countdown motif): 'Massive circular steel vault door in a dark concrete room, locking bolts retracting one by one, warm light leaking through the seams. Camera: slow push-in to the centre. Cold top light, floating dust. 35mm, deep shadows, metallic textures, subtle grain. Vertical 9:16.'
For Hailuo, test appending a bracketed command such as [Push in].

DISCLOSURE: turn on each platform's AI-content disclosure for photorealistic AI clips and leave provenance metadata intact. Stripping it to avoid labels is a policy risk; the details belong to the policy stream.

research.summary: Rockstar's fan-content policy only covers 'occasional, non-commercial' fan use. It excludes ads, film/TV and publishing uses, and it says leaked or pre-release footage, spoilers, and isolated cutscenes or in-game TV clips get removed. So any Rockstar footage on a monetized account is tolerated at best and can be withdrawn; it is never licensed. (I could not read the policy's full monetization wording this session.) Take-Two enforces hard: it cleared the 2022 GTA 6 leak videos with takedowns (strikes, not Content ID claims), and in August 2026 it reportedly won DMCA subpoenas to identify the people who uploaded GTA 6 leaks. In launch week, leaked, early-copy or datamined material can cost the account. The safest setup is the reference creator's: an original brand like 'Unseen.' with no GTA, Rockstar or VI in the @handle and no official logo or art as the avatar. Use 'GTA 6' only to describe the topic in the display name, bio and captions, and add a line saying the account is not affiliated with Rockstar Games or Take-Two (Instagram's terms let it change usernames that infringe IP or impersonate). All three platforms require realistic AI to be disclosed. Meta's rule covers photoreal video and realistic-sounding audio, which includes both the Higgsfield clips and the ElevenLabs voice. YouTube's covers realistic synthetic scenes and synthetic narration voices, and TikTok's covers realistic AI-generated content. Platforms can apply labels automatically when they detect provenance data or watermarks, and skipping disclosure can lead to removal or YouTube Partner Program penalties. Never present AI renders as real gameplay, leaks or trailers, which breaks YouTube's rules on misleading titles and thumbnails, and do not generate close copies of Jason, Lucia, the GTA VI logo or the HUD, since those would be derivative works. Keep commercial music out of the ffmpeg master, especially the trailer songs (Tom Petty, The Pointer Sisters). Add trending sounds only inside each app on a non-business account, and use royalty-free tracks on YouTube and in anything sponsored. On YouTube, an 81-second Short with any Content ID claim is reportedly blocked worldwide, so YouTube cuts must be claim-free or 60 seconds or shorter, and should be checked with YouTube Studio 'Checks' before publishing. US fair use protects brief stills you comment on better than trailer B-roll used as background, but automated matching ignores fair use, and a counter-notice against Take-Two reveals your identity. Monetization programs now penalize templated, mass-produced or unoriginal content (YouTube's 'inauthentic content' rule since July 2025, plus Meta's and TikTok's originality rules), so each daily episode needs new research, a new script and new visuals.

findings.claim: Rockstar's 'Policy on posting copyrighted Rockstar Games material' frames its permission as addressing 'occasional, non-commercial in-game content use by individual members of the fan community'. It states it does not cover use of Rockstar IP for film/TV/streaming distribution, music videos, advertisements, or books, magazines and digital publishing.
findings.note: Text taken from the search index of the official page on 2026-11-12. I could not fetch the page directly because support.rockstargames.com is not in this session's network allowlist, so I have not read the full wording or the last-updated date.

findings.claim: The same policy says pre-release or leaked footage is removed and spoiler videos can be taken down. Isolated cinematics or in-game TV shows/comedy posted on their own are flagged for removal. Rockstar reserves the right to have its material taken down at any time and to change the policy. Questions go to copyright@take2games.com.
findings.note: Same extraction caveat. Launch-week press is covering Rockstar's GTA 6 spoiler/video takedown policy (tbreak.com headline 'gta-6-spoilers-rockstar-video-takedown-policy'), but I could not read that article (host blocked).

findings.claim: The policy text I could retrieve does not expressly allow monetizing videos that contain Rockstar material. One secondary summary reads 'non-commercial' as 'you don't make money from the footage'. Ad-monetized GTA gameplay channels are common, so monetization looks tolerated and revocable rather than licensed.
findings.note: Exact monetization wording not read. Ask copyright@take2games.com in writing before building revenue on Rockstar footage.

findings.claim: Rockstar has published rules on using game footage since at least GTA V's launch (Sept 2013), so the current policy is long-standing and not specific to GTA 6.
After the September 2022 breach, in which about 90 GTA 6 development clips were posted, Take-Two filed removal notices that cleared the YouTube copies.
findings.note: Takedown detail comes from a search summary; the Guardian piece covers the breach itself.

findings.claim: Take-Two issued a takedown notice against a Goat Simulator video that used the GTA 6 leaks, so enforcement reached even a game studio's parody.
findings.note: Known from the headline only. I recall it as 2022 (Goat Simulator 3 marketing), but did not re-check the date.

findings.claim: Leaked GTA 6 footage on YouTube has drawn DMCA takedowns, which are copyright strikes, rather than Content ID claims. That means penalties at the account level, not just lost revenue.
findings.note: Lower-tier blog, but consistent with the 2022 enforcement pattern.

findings.claim: In August 2026 Take-Two filed four DMCA subpoena applications over new GTA 6 leaks, and two were granted. They sought account information from Discord, Microsoft, X and Google. Take-Two is now identifying uploaders, not only removing posts.
findings.note: Also covered by cybermagazine.com/news/gta-vi-footage-leak-and-take-twos-legal-fightback-explained. Read via search summaries only. Claims that the 2026 leaker is 'Cyberleek' and that Take-Two lost about $2.83B in market value come from low-quality sites (tech-insider.org, shattered.io) and are unverified.

findings.claim: The Discord of the fan-run GTA 6 Mapping Project, which had shared leaks, disappeared in 2026 amid suspected Take-Two action. The cause is unconfirmed.

Take-Two's wider record includes suing the re3/reVC reverse-engineering developers (2021), shutting down large mods (e.g., the Liberty City Preservation Project, Jan 2025) and the removal of a mod team's YouTube channel (Vice City Nextgen Edition). It removes whole channels, not just individual videos.
findings.source_url: not retrieved this session (prior knowledge, search budget exhausted)

findings.claim: YouTube reportedly updated its ad rules for graphic video-game violence ahead of GTA 6. According to coverage, graphic violence in the first seconds (reported as the first ~7 s) stays ineligible for ads, while graphic gameplay later in the video (reported as from about 8 s on) can earn.
findings.note: Also covered by Express Tribune (tribune.com.pk/story/2627692, around Sept 2026). The thresholds come from a search summary; verify them in YouTube's advertiser-friendly guidelines.

findings.claim: GTA 6 is scheduled for November 19, 2026 on PS5 and Xbox Series X|S. Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick has repeated the date publicly, including on an earnings call. No PC version has been announced.
findings.note: Also covered by respawn.outlookindia.com. I did not read Rockstar Newswire directly.

findings.claim: Instagram's Terms of Use say you can't impersonate others, and Instagram may change a username if it 'infringes someone's intellectual property or impersonates another user'.
findings.note: Wording is from the published Terms as of my last knowledge; not re-fetched. Rights owners can also report through Meta's IP and brand-protection channels, so a handle containing the trademark can be reported even if no post infringes.

findings.claim: US nominative fair use allows naming a trademarked product to refer to it if (1) it can't readily be identified otherwise, (2) only as much of the mark as needed is used (the plain words, not the logo or stylized lettering), and (3) nothing suggests sponsorship. This supports writing 'GTA 6' in captions and bios, but not using logos or 'official'-style names.
findings.source_url: New Kids on the Block v. News America Publishing, 971 F.2d 302 (9th Cir. 1992); URL not retrieved
findings.note: Applying this to social handles is my own analysis. Platforms enforce their own rules regardless of the legal defense.

findings.claim: TikTok's impersonation rules allow fan, commentary and parody accounts only if they don't mislead about who runs them. Such accounts are expected to say so clearly, e.g., 'fan' or 'unofficial' in the name or bio.
findings.note: Exact current wording after the 2025 guidelines refresh not re-verified.

findings.claim: YouTube's impersonation policy bans channels that copy another channel's or organization's name, image or overall look, including near-identical names.
findings.note: Not re-fetched this session.

findings.claim: Take-Two/Rockstar hold the GRAND THEFT AUTO, GTA and ROCKSTAR GAMES trademarks and logo artwork, including the GTA VI logo.
findings.source_url: not looked up (USPTO TSDR / EUIPO eSearch)
findings.note: Check registrations before final naming.

findings.claim: Meta requires people to use its AI disclosure tool when posting organic content with photorealistic video or realistic-sounding audio that was digitally created or altered, and says it may apply penalties if they don't.
findings.note: Applied here, this covers photoreal Higgsfield clips and an ElevenLabs voice clone, even of your own voice. There is no exemption for self-clones.

findings.claim: Meta also labels content automatically when it detects industry-standard AI signals (C2PA/IPTC metadata). The label was renamed 'AI info' (July 2024), and for content only edited with AI it moved into the post menu (Sept 2024).
findings.note: The rename and menu-placement updates are from later revisions of this post, as I recall them; not re-fetched.

findings.claim: YouTube requires disclosure of realistic altered or synthetic content. Its examples include 'synthetically generating a person's voice to narrate a video' and realistic scenes that did not happen. Clearly unrealistic or animated content, filters, and AI help with scripts, ideas or captions are exempt. Creators who consistently fail to disclose can face removals or suspension from the YouTube Partner Program.
findings.note: Example wording dates from the March 2024 rollout. Whether near-photoreal GTA-style renders count as 'animation' is a gray area, so disclose.

findings.claim: TikTok requires a label on AI-generated content showing realistic scenes, people or audio, either with the 'AI-generated content' toggle or a clear caption, sticker or watermark. Since May 2024 it automatically labels uploads that carry C2PA Content Credentials, and it may label or remove realistic AI content that isn't labeled.
findings.note: That a caption or sticker also counts, and the removal wording, are from the Community Guidelines as of my last knowledge; not re-fetched.

findings.claim: TikTok said in November 2025 it would let users turn down how much AI-generated content they see (a control in 'Manage topics') and expand invisible watermarking. Labeled AI content may reach fewer people who opt out.
YouTube's spam and deceptive-practices policy prohibits misleading metadata and thumbnails. Titling AI renders as 'leaked gameplay', 'official trailer' or 'real footage' would fall under it.
findings.note: The policy is confirmed. Applying it to AI GTA renders is my analysis (estimate).

findings.claim: Copyright protects distinctive characters and their designs. Close AI replicas of Jason or Lucia, the GTA VI logo, or the HUD (minimap, wanted stars, 'WASTED' screen) would be derivative of Take-Two's protected expression and trade dress. Being AI-made is no defense.
findings.source_url: DC Comics v. Towle, 802 F.3d 1012 (9th Cir. 2015); URL not retrieved
findings.note: My legal analysis. Generic Florida/neon/vice-city-style imagery without those specific elements carries far less risk.

findings.claim: Re-encoding with ffmpeg usually drops C2PA manifests, but invisible watermarks embedded by some video models (e.g., Google's SynthID on Veo outputs) can survive. Platforms that read these signals can auto-label content, so not disclosing is unreliable as well as against policy.
findings.note: Which Higgsfield-hosted models embed C2PA or watermarks is an open question.

findings.claim: EU AI Act Art. 50(4): anyone who professionally uses AI to generate or manipulate image, audio or video 'deep fakes' must disclose it. Deep fakes are defined as content resembling existing persons, objects, places, entities or events that would falsely appear authentic. For evidently artistic, creative or fictional works the duty shrinks to a non-intrusive disclosure. Personal non-professional use is outside the definition. Art. 50 applies from 2 August 2026.
findings.note: Official text: eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj. Relevant only if the user is EU-based. I could not check whether the EU 'Digital Omnibus' proposal has since changed Art. 50 timelines.

findings.claim: The US Copyright Office says purely AI-generated material is not copyrightable. Human-written scripts, narration and the creative selection and arrangement of an edit can be.
findings.note: The Part 2 report is from January 2025. Consequence: copycats can reuse the raw AI shots, but the script and edit are protectable.

findings.claim: Ideas, formats, methods, names, titles and short phrases are not copyrightable, and neither are facts (Feist). Copying the reference creator's countdown format and maths-based hooks is lawful; copying its caption text, sign-off line or branding is not advisable.
findings.note: Feist v. Rural, 499 U.S. 340 (1991): supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/499/340/. A sign-off line used as a brand can still raise impersonation or trademark-style complaints.

findings.claim: Meta's Music Guidelines say using music for commercial or non-personal purposes is prohibited unless you have the appropriate licenses.

Instagram Business accounts are limited to a royalty-free sound collection, while Creator and personal accounts get the wider licensed library, and only for non-commercial use inside the app. Branded or paid-partnership posts need commercially licensed music.
findings.note: The difference between Business and Creator libraries is from Instagram help and press as I recall them; not re-verified.

findings.claim: TikTok Business accounts can only use the Commercial Music Library. The Creator Rewards Program (as of 2025) requires a personal account, age 18+, 10k followers, 100k views in the last 30 days, and original videos longer than 1 minute in eligible countries.
findings.source_url: not retrieved (TikTok Help Center: Creator Rewards Program; Commercial Music Library)
findings.note: Prior knowledge; criteria may have changed by Nov 2026. The 81-second format clears the 1-minute bar.

findings.claim: In YouTube Shorts revenue sharing, using music shrinks the creator pool's share (one track halves it, two tracks cut it to a third), and creators receive 45% of their allocated revenue.
findings.note: Not re-fetched this session.

findings.claim: Since October 2024 Shorts can run up to 3 minutes, but Shorts longer than 1 minute with an active Content ID claim are blocked globally.
findings.source_url: not retrieved (YouTube Help, Shorts length update, Oct 2024)
findings.note: This matters a lot here: an 81 s Short containing any claimed trailer clip or song would be blocked. Confirm the rule is unchanged in Nov 2026.

findings.claim: GTA 6 Trailer 1 used Tom Petty's 'Love Is a Long Road' and Trailer 2 used The Pointer Sisters' 'Hot Together'. Both are third-party recordings licensed by Rockstar, so reusing trailer audio risks matches by music rights holders regardless of Rockstar's own tolerance.
findings.note: The song identities are widely reported. The claim risk is my estimate. GTA's in-game radio is similarly licensed, so mute it when capturing gameplay after launch.

findings.claim: Content ID and Rights Manager risk for official trailer clips, ranked (estimate): trailer audio = high (music fingerprinting); trailer video = medium/unknown (whether Rockstar uses Content ID or Rights Manager is unverified); annotated stills without audio = low. On YouTube, Shorts over 60 s with any claim are reportedly blocked worldwide. Meta Rights Manager lets owners block or monitor matching Reels (and claim ad earnings on Facebook).
findings.note: Test before publishing: upload privately to YouTube and wait for Studio 'Checks'.

findings.claim: US fair use weighs four factors, and comment, criticism and news reporting are the listed favored purposes. Commercial use alone is not decisive (Campbell, 1994), but after Warhol v. Goldsmith (2023) a commercial use that serves substantially the same purpose as the original weighs against fair use. Trailer clips used as hype B-roll are weak; brief frames that you actually analyze are stronger.
findings.note: Statute: law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/107. Campbell: supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/510/569/. There is no safe-harbor number of seconds. Outside the US, only narrower quotation, review and parody exceptions apply.

findings.claim: YouTube says it cannot decide fair use, and Content ID matching runs automatically. Three copyright strikes within 90 days terminate a channel. A DMCA counter-notice must include your name, address and phone and consent to US federal court jurisdiction, and it is forwarded to the claimant.
findings.note: Strike rules: support.google.com/youtube/answer/2814000. Counter-notice requirements: 17 U.S.C. 512(g)(3), law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/512. Take-Two has litigated against fan projects before (re3), so counter-noticing it is risky.

findings.claim: In July 2025 YouTube renamed its 'repetitious content' monetization rule to 'inauthentic content', targeting mass-produced or repetitive videos (e.g., templated with little variation). Reused-content rules still apply.
findings.note: A daily templated series of AI visuals with a cloned voice is exactly what reviewers look at, so each episode needs to be substantively distinct.

findings.claim: Meta's originality enforcement: Instagram (April 2024) said reposted content would be replaced by the original in recommendations and repeat aggregators demoted. Facebook (July 2025) said accounts that repeatedly reuse others' content lose monetization and distribution. Meta's monetization policies require rights to the content you monetize.
findings.note: The URL is Meta's Partner Monetization Policies page as I know it; the announcement URLs were not retrieved.

findings.claim: The FTC Endorsement Guides require clear disclosure of material connections such as sponsorships, free codes and affiliate links, including on short-form video.
ElevenLabs' pricing lists Instant Voice Cloning and a commercial license starting at the paid Starter tier. The free tier is not for commercial use.
findings.note: From the pricing page as I last knew it; not re-fetched. Confirm the user's plan.

examples.name: Unseen. (@unseenbyneuralway), reference reel DfmB1XwqUB-
examples.what_works: An IP-light pattern worth copying in structure. The brand name contains no Rockstar or Take-Two trademark. The hook rests on facts and the creator's own arithmetic (2^128 maths), which nobody owns, and the caption separates 'our arithmetic / on the record / measured / estimate', which also guards against misinformation flags. Copy the pattern, not the words: its name and its sign-off line ('the part of GTA 6 you never see') are its brand assets.
examples.metrics: 22,289 likes and 149 comments on 2026-11-12 (from the brief); views not exposed. I did not check whether its visuals include Rockstar footage.

examples.name: Long-running fan brands: GTAForums/GTANet, Rockstar Intel, GTA BOOM
examples.what_works: They name themselves 'trademark + generic word' (Forums, Intel, BOOM), present as news or community, and never claim to be official. This shows descriptive use of the mark can last for years. It fits a brand-new IG/TikTok account in launch week less well: 'GTA 6 + word' handles are crowded with spam and scam accounts and are easy trademark-report targets (my estimate).
examples.metrics: Not measured; their disclaimers and legal history were not checked this session.

examples.name: Counterexample: Goat Simulator video using GTA 6 leaks
examples.what_works: What fails: Take-Two had even a game studio's joke video built on leaked GTA 6 footage taken down. Calling it parody or reaction does not protect content derived from leaks.
examples.metrics: Takedown issued (reported).

examples.name: Counterexample: GTA 6 Mapping Project, 2026
examples.what_works: What fails: a fan analysis community that circulated leaks lost its Discord amid suspected Take-Two action (cause unconfirmed). Communities close to leaks are enforcement targets even when the main project is legitimate fan work.
examples.metrics: Discord closed (reported).

recommendations: DO choose an original, ownable brand with no 'GTA', 'Rockstar', 'VI' or 'Official' in the @handle (the reference's 'Unseen.' pattern) and use the same handle on IG, TikTok and YT. Use 'GTA 6' only as a descriptive keyword in the display name, bio, captions and hashtags (e.g., '<Brand> | GTA 6 explained'). Basis: the Instagram ToS username clause and nominative fair use.

DO put this in every bio: 'Unofficial fan channel. Not affiliated with or endorsed by Rockstar Games or Take-Two. Visuals AI-generated; narration is my own AI voice clone.' It covers TikTok's fan-account signaling and impersonation rules and gives a standing AI disclosure. Per-post labels are still required.
DON'T use the R* logo, GTA VI logo or key art, official character renders, Rockstar-style logo lockups, or the words 'Official', 'Leaks' or 'Insider' in the avatar, banner, watermark or name.

DON'T copy the reference creator's name, sign-off ('the part of GTA 6 you never see'), caption text or visual identity. Formats, ideas and facts are free to use (Copyright Office Circular 33; Feist); its expression and branding are not. Write your own recurring sign-off.

DON'T touch leaked, early-copy (street-date-break), pre-release or datamined GTA 6 material in any form: repost, reaction, blur, recreation, 'analysis' or link. This applies especially in launch week. Rockstar's policy removes it, and Take-Two uses strikes and, since Aug 2026, DMCA subpoenas to identify uploaders.

DO make every reel free of Rockstar assets by default: original AI concept visuals, your narration, and facts or numbers you can source. This is also the only reliable way to keep 61-180 s YouTube Shorts free of claims.

IF you use official material: use still frames from Rockstar's own releases, on screen only while you comment on them, credited 'Rockstar Games'. No trailer audio, no full trailer, no cutscene-only or in-game TV clips, and no story spoilers. Treat this as tolerated, not licensed, and email copyright@take2games.com before scaling revenue on it.

DO upload YouTube versions privately first and wait for Studio 'Checks'. Any Content ID claim on a Short over 60 s reportedly blocks it worldwide, so cut to 60 s or less or remove the claimed element before publishing.

DON'T counter-notify a Take-Two takedown unless the material is entirely yours. A DMCA counter-notice discloses your name and address and consents to US court jurisdiction. Three YouTube strikes within 90 days terminate the channel, and on a new account a single strike also hurts recommendation eligibility.

DO turn on the AI label for every post with photoreal AI visuals or the cloned voice: Instagram 'AI label' (Advanced settings), TikTok 'AI-generated content', YouTube 'Altered or synthetic content: Yes'. Don't count on ffmpeg re-encoding to avoid detection; watermarks and auto-labels make hiding unreliable, and non-disclosure is penalized.

DO add a short on-screen note, 'AI visualization, not game footage', whenever an AI shot could pass for real GTA 6 footage. DON'T title or thumbnail AI renders as 'gameplay', 'leaked', 'official', 'Trailer 3' or 'confirmed'; that breaks YouTube's misleading-metadata rules and Meta's and TikTok's AI rules.

DON'T prompt for close replicas of Jason, Lucia, the GTA VI logo, the HUD (minimap, wanted stars, 'WASTED' screen) or real people such as Rockstar staff, voice actors or executives. Use original characters and settings that are inspired by Florida or Vice City without copying the game.

DON'T clone or imitate any voice except your own. Keep ElevenLabs on a paid tier with a commercial license. Keep project files, prompts, Higgsfield job IDs and ElevenLabs history as proof of originality for disputes and monetization reviews.

DO keep the ffmpeg master clean: narration, sound effects and owned or royalty-free music only. Add trending sounds inside Instagram or TikTok, low under the voice, on Creator or personal accounts. Never cross-post an export that has one platform's licensed song baked into it.
DON'T use the trailer songs (Tom Petty 'Love Is a Long Road', The Pointer Sisters 'Hot Together') or GTA radio tracks. After launch, capture gameplay with the in-game radio muted.

DO use only commercially licensed music (Meta Sound Collection, TikTok Commercial Music Library, YouTube Audio Library, or a paid sync license) in any sponsored or paid-partnership post. Avoid Business account types on IG and TikTok if you want the full trending library; TikTok's Creator Rewards Program also needs a personal account.

DO make each countdown episode substantively new (research, script and shots), not one template with swapped text. YouTube's 'inauthentic content' rule (July 2025), Meta's unoriginal-content rules and TikTok's Creator Rewards originality rules all gate monetization.
DO keep graphic violence out of the first seconds of YouTube uploads (reported 2026 ad-rule update). This matters for gameplay clips after Nov 19.
DO disclose affiliate links, free codes and sponsorships with each platform's paid-partnership tool plus '#ad' (FTC Endorsement Guides; similar rules in the UK and EU).
DON'T run 'free GTA 6 / beta / early access' giveaways or post download links. It is a classic scam pattern and breaks spam and promotion rules (my estimate).
IF EU-based: the same AI labels plus the on-screen note satisfy EU AI Act Art. 50(4) deepfake disclosure, which has applied since 2 Aug 2026.

research.summary: Platforms are not throttling AI content for being AI in 2026. They are throttling unoriginal content. Instagram stops recommending accounts that mostly post other people's content to non-followers. That has applied to Reels since 2024 and was extended to photos and carousels on 30 Apr 2026 (reported). Instagram's own guidance says stitching clips together or adding a watermark is not a material edit. That matters a lot for a zero-follower account, because all of its early reach has to come from recommendations. All three platforms expect you to disclose realistic AI visuals and synthetic voices, and Meta and TikTok also label uploads that carry C2PA tags automatically. Mosseri reportedly says labeled AI is not held back for being AI (exact wording unverified). However, TikTok now lets viewers turn AI content down, YouTube's inauthentic-content policy and reported enforcement waves target mass-produced AI channels, and fake AI movie-trailer channels lost YouTube monetization (reported). That makes 'GTA 6 AI trailer' or 'leak' content the riskiest format by far. The pattern that breaks out, both in the reference reel and in big faceless explainer channels, is a scripted, research-heavy series with a human voice. The first word comes in under 0.2 s, delivery runs at about 185 words per minute, there is a cut every 6 s or so and a re-hook near the halfway point, and the series ends on a short fixed sign-off. The caption carries the exact figures and labels what is on the record versus what is an estimate. In that format the AI visuals illustrate the story; they are not the product. The user's own cloned voice is the main originality and identity asset. Clone it from a sample recorded at full reel energy (the clone copies the sample's delivery), keep it private, and drive the ffmpeg captions from the text-to-speech word timestamps. For visuals, generate images first under a fixed style guide and add all numbers and text in ffmpeg. Avoid AI faces, Rockstar characters and anything that looks like real gameplay or real events, and add a few real self-shot clips to each reel, which fits Instagram's 2026 push to verify authentic media and show who is behind accounts. Make reels people want to send and repost (Instagram reposts now push your reel to the reposter's followers), test hooks with Trial Reels where the account has them, and watch the 3-second skip rate, sends per reach and Account Status daily during launch week. Keep master edits at 61-90 s so they qualify for TikTok Creator Rewards (over 1 min, 10k followers, 100k views in 30 days) and YouTube Shorts. Keep any Rockstar footage or music that Content ID could claim out of Shorts longer than 60 s, because those get blocked worldwide. Evidence caveat: this stream used up the shared web-search budget after five queries, and most sites were blocked by the session's network. The 2026 items rest on trade-press and blog reports, and several tool and case-study figures come from my training knowledge (up to mid-2026). Those are flagged for re-checking.

findings.claim: [Instagram originality, primary source] Instagram says it is less likely to recommend reposts of a reel already on Instagram, content with noticeable watermarks, or accounts that regularly collect and reshare others' content.
findings.note: Seen as a search extract this session; the page itself could not be fetched here. Visible watermarks from AI generators, CapCut end cards or the TikTok logo all fall under this rule.

findings.claim: [Instagram originality, primary source] Instagram: 'Simply stitching together clips or adding a watermark does not qualify as materially edited content.'
findings.note: Quoted in a search extract. It may be on this 'About original content' help page or on the creators blog; I could not tell which. Meta used the same test in its July 2025 Facebook rule on unoriginal content.

findings.claim: [Instagram eligibility, primary source] An account that repeatedly posts content breaking the Recommendation Guidelines, or has violating elements in its profile, can be made ineligible for recommendations for a period, with none of its content recommended. Account Status shows whether an account is eligible.
findings.note: For an account with 0 followers, losing eligibility means almost no reach.

findings.claim: [Instagram 2026] On 30 Apr 2026 Instagram extended its anti-aggregator penalty from Reels to photos and carousels. Mosseri said: 'If most of what you post to Instagram is someone else's content, your account is no longer going to be recommendable.' Followers still see these accounts' posts, but the posts are not recommended to non-followers. Changing a video's speed or adding a screenshot credit to the original poster is not enough.
findings.note: Tubefilter (30 Apr 2026) and MarketingEdge reported the same. Mosseri suggested aggregators remix content, use the repost button or make collab posts instead. www.tubefilter.com is blocked by this session's network and needs to be allowed before it can be fetched; I read it only through search extracts.

findings.claim: [Instagram mechanics] A commonly cited Reels rule from Instagram's April 2024 ranking update says accounts that post other people's content 10 or more times in 30 days lose recommendations, and that when identical copies exist only the original is recommended.

It says Instagram will explore clearer AI labels, ways to verify ('fingerprint') authentic media, and showing more information about the accounts behind posts. He also expects platforms to get worse at detecting AI over time.

More prominent automatic labels are reportedly planned, and an account-level AI label reportedly launched in 2026.

It also applies the 'AI info' label automatically when it detects C2PA or IPTC signals.

Voice Changer (speech-to-speech) converts your own reading into the clone while keeping your timing. Eleven v3 adds inline audio tags such as [excited] or [whispers].

It re-hooks at about 49%, pays off, and ends on a fixed branded sign-off. The daily numbered countdown gives people a reason to follow. The long caption sorts claims into our arithmetic / on the record / measured / estimate, which earns trust despite the AI visuals.

recommendations: Originality floor: post only your own edits. That means no reposted reels, no re-uploaded trailers, no other creators' clips, and no visible third-party watermarks (generator logos, CapCut end cards, the TikTok logo). Check Instagram Account Status for recommendation eligibility every few days; with 0 followers, one eligibility strike wipes out launch-week reach.

Copy the structure of the Unseen. reels, not the surface. Use your own series name, tagline, sign-off, caption layout, colour palette and angles. Reuse only the beat order: a line addressed to the viewer (0-3 s), a number shock (by about 8 s), stakes and history, a re-hook at 45-55%, the payoff, then a fixed 3-4 s sign-off with the day number.

Script spec: make master edits 61-90 s long, about 190-280 words at about 185 wpm. TikTok Creator Rewards needs more than 60 s, and Reels and Shorts allow up to 3 minutes. The first spoken word should land within 0.2 s, with no intro or logo animation. Include one surprising, checkable fact per reel that people will want to send to a friend. Give every episode new substance so a daily series never looks repetitive or mass-produced to YouTube.

The narration rounds numbers; the caption carries the evidence. Put exact numbers, the method, labeled claim types (on the record / measured / our estimate) and named sources in the caption. Start the caption with search keywords (e.g. 'GTA 6 preload size...'), because Instagram captions feed Instagram and Google search, and TikTok and YouTube search rely on captions and titles.

Disclose AI everywhere. Turn on Instagram's AI label, TikTok's 'AI-generated' toggle, and YouTube's 'altered or synthetic' setting (it covers realistic scenes and a synthetic voice of a real person). Put 'AI-assisted visuals, my own cloned voice, sources in caption' in the bio. Never present AI imagery as real GTA 6 footage, leaks, trailers or real events, and never show AI versions of Rockstar or Sony staff, offices or apologies. Avoid any name that could read as official, such as 'Rockstar' or 'Official'.

Voice, today: create an ElevenLabs Instant Voice Clone from 1-2 minutes of clean audio recorded at full reel energy, because the clone copies the delivery of the sample. If the account takes off after launch week, record 30 minutes to 3 hours for a Professional Voice Clone. Keep the voice private (don't share it in the Voice Library) and turn on two-factor login: the voice is the brand.

Voice-sample script (the user offered to record one). Record in a quiet room with soft furnishings, using the same mic and the same 15-20 cm distance you will always use. No music, fans or noise-suppression filters; save as WAV at 44.1-48 kHz; make sure nothing clips. Read it twice, once at full reel pace and once a notch calmer, cut out long pauses, and upload the best 60-120 s. Text: 'Okay, stop scrolling for one second. Tonight, millions of consoles are doing something nobody talks about. Fans spinning. Drives filling up. A whole map, sitting there, silent. Why? Because one tiny file hasn't arrived yet. So here's what's actually going on. Three hundred and forty undecillion. Thirty-nine digits. One point two billion. Two hundred and twelve gigabytes. Fifty percent. Twenty thirteen. Twenty twenty-two. Twenty twenty-six. November nineteenth. Rockstar. Leonida. Vice City. Jason and Lucia. PlayStation 5. Xbox Series X. Preload. Encryption. Decryption key. Did you catch all of that? Good. Now a little quieter, like you're telling a friend a secret: nobody can play it yet. Not even close. And now back up, full energy: the second that key lands, the whole map wakes up, and millions of people press start at the exact same moment. See you tomorrow.' This is sample text only; the numbers are pronunciation practice, not claims.

Text-to-speech technique: generate the audio one paragraph at a time, not the whole script. Write numbers as words. Add pronunciation rules (GTA VI as 'G T A six', Leonida, Lucia). Start with stability around 0.45, similarity 0.75 and style 0. If a line comes out with the wrong emphasis, record it yourself and convert it with Voice Changer. Reach about 185 wpm by tightening the script and trimming gaps with ffmpeg silenceremove, or atempo at no more than 1.1, rather than maxing out the TTS speed.

Captions from timestamps: use ElevenLabs 'with timestamps' (or Scribe/WhisperX) to build an ASS subtitle file that highlights each word, 1-3 words per chunk, and burn it in with ffmpeg's subtitles filter (libass). Keep text in the middle band of the frame, away from the bottom ~25% and right ~15% where the app buttons sit. Rename the Instagram original audio to the series name so anyone reusing it advertises the account.

Visual system: write a style guide with 3-4 recurring motifs (for example console, lock or vault, key, city lights), one colour palette, one font and a small logo mark. Apply one colour grade (LUT) and film grain in ffmpeg to make outputs from different models match. Generate style-matched still images first using reference images, animate them into 5-8 s clips, and cut those to 4-7 s. Plan about 13-15 shots per 80 s.

Never let the AI draw text, digits or logos; add exact numbers and labels with ffmpeg drawtext or ASS. Avoid obvious AI flaws (close-up AI faces and hands, morphing, warped text) and regenerate any shot that has them. Commenters screenshot these flaws, and 'AI slop' replies hurt trust.

Mix real footage into each reel: your console's preload or download screen, a store shelf, your own charts or screen recordings. It can't be faked, it is original, it is cheaper than generating, and it fits Instagram's 2026 push to verify authentic media and show who is behind accounts.

Rockstar material: on Instagram and TikTok, use only short clips, edited and placed under your own commentary. On YouTube, a Short over 60 s with any Content ID claim is blocked worldwide, so keep Shorts over 60 s free of Rockstar material or publish a cut of 60 s or less. Never use songs from the GTA soundtrack, and don't feed trailer frames into image-to-video.

Export and upload: 1080x1920, 30 fps, H.264 High (CRF 16-18 or about 10-16 Mbps), AAC audio at 48 kHz. Aim for about -14 LUFS loudness with true peak at or below -1 dB, and duck music 15-20 dB under the voice (sidechaincompress). No borders. Turn on Instagram's 'Upload at highest quality' setting, and upload directly to each platform on the same day.

Test and measure: make two hook versions per script and test them with Trial Reels on Instagram if the account has them, otherwise compare across platforms. Track the 3-second skip rate, average % watched, sends per reach and follows per reach. When the skip rate is bad, change the hook formula, not the series.

Distribution: invite established GTA creators to Collab posts, and make countdown reels worth reposting (Instagram reposts carry your reel to the reposter's followers). Turn on Meta AI translations (English/Spanish) for Reels, and later consider Spanish and Portuguese versions on TikTok and YouTube using the multilingual clone. Avoid explicit 'share this' or 'comment X' bait, and never buy followers or join engagement pods.

Posting rhythm: one countdown episode every day at a fixed time until launch (reported as 19 Nov 2026), plus quick reactive reels on major launch news. After launch, keep a daily series going for at least 30 days so the TikTok thresholds (10k followers, 100k views in 30 days) and YouTube thresholds (1k subscribers plus 10M Shorts views in 90 days) are within reach.

What makes accounts stall: templated 'top 10 facts' lists, re-uploaded trailers, 'LEAKED' or fake AI trailer bait, stock-sounding TTS voices, several near-identical reels or accounts, unlabeled AI, inconsistent branding, and slow intros.

Higgsfield: check the current models and the credit cost per 5-8 s clip in the app before setting a daily budget. Use the toolset's virality predictor only as a first filter, and trust real skip-rate and sends data over it.

research.summary: On a brand-new Instagram account almost all reach comes from non-followers. Mosseri names watch time, likes per reach and sends per reach as Instagram's top three ranking signals, and says sends count slightly more with non-followers. So every script should be built to be watched to the end and to have one payoff worth sending to a friend. Comment-keyword DM automations mainly build a contact list; they are not a reach tactic. The first 3 seconds are now measured directly: Instagram added Skip Rate and a second-by-second Retention chart to Reels Insights around August 2025, and YouTube shows Viewed vs Swiped away. Meta and TikTok ad research puts roughly half of a video's measured impact in the first 2-3 seconds. So the hook must be finished by about 2.5 s in both voice and on-screen text, with speech starting by 0.2 s and no intro. The reference reel's measurable recipe: about 3 words per second, sentences of about 3.2 s, the first big number by about 9 s, a 'here's the part' style rehook at about 49% of runtime, history and stakes at about 62-88%, the payoff at about 90-95%, and an ending that calls back to the opening line. A 45-60 s version therefore needs 135-180 words in the same proportions. The best-evidenced hook mechanics are: a specific gap in knowledge about a topic viewers half-know (Loewenstein 1994; Kang et al. 2009); speaking to the viewer as 'you'; awe or anxiety, which drive sharing (Berger & Milkman 2012); one honest negative stakes word (each extra negative word raised clicks 2.3% in Upworthy's headline tests); and big numbers restated at human scale. Put the strongest moment at the end, because people judge an experience mostly by its peak and its ending (the peak-end rule). The best shot and the payoff go at 80-92%, the CTA and your own sign-off only in the final 2-4 s, and the last frame should match frame 1, because Instagram and YouTube Shorts both count replays as views. Run a countdown from 7 days out (today) to launch day, Nov 19, then a renamed daily count-up for at least 8-10 weeks. Anticipation and the push of a near goal peak before launch, but habits take a median of 66 days to form. Copy the reference's structure, not its surface: use your own series name, hook wording and sign-off. Keep a labeled 'receipts' caption (on the record / reported / our math / estimate), which also enforces the no-rumor rule. The shared web-search budget ran out mid-stream and most sites were blocked by the network allowlist. So the GTA 6 facts behind the example hooks, and some platform details, come from knowledge up to mid-2026 and must be re-checked against Rockstar's site and newswire before posting. On the user's offer to record a voice sample: the filled 55-second example script plus the five GTA 6 hooks make a 1.5-2 minute read in the target reel style. That suits Instant Voice Cloning; ElevenLabs suggests roughly 1-2 minutes of clean audio, though that guidance was not re-checked this session.

findings.claim: Adam Mosseri (Jan 2025 video) named watch time, likes and sends as Instagram's top three ranking signals, told creators to watch average watch time, likes per reach and sends per reach, and said likes weigh slightly more for connected (follower) content while sends weigh slightly more for unconnected (non-follower) content.
findings.note: Quotes surfaced via search: 'The top three signals that matter most for ranking are watch time, likes and sends' and 'Likes are slightly more important for connected content, and sends are slightly more important for unconnected content.' Page could not be opened (host not in network allowlist). Search summaries also carried an earlier Mosseri Q&A line that sends per reach 'correlate more ... with overall reach than anything else' (originating page not identified). A new account's reach is almost all unconnected, so sends per reach is the lever; historically creators had to compute it as shares / accounts reached.

findings.claim: Instagram added a second-by-second Retention chart and a Skip Rate metric to Reels Insights (coverage dated Aug 25, 2025). Skip Rate = share of views that skip within the first 3 seconds (views skipped in 3 s / initial views), replacing View Rate; Instagram publishes no benchmark and skip rate is reportedly labeled an estimated metric.
findings.note: Also covered by socialsamosa.com, wersm.com, metricool.com. Search summaries also surfaced a Mosseri line from an Instagram Reel: 'The first three seconds of a reel are super important' (originating page not identified).

findings.claim: A third-party write-up says Instagram's April 2026 Insights update split Insights into Overview, Engagement and Audience tabs and added share rate and views over time.
findings.note: Vendor blog, not Instagram. If accurate, sends per reach can be tracked natively; check in the app.

findings.claim: Instagram's current Views metric counts every play including replays and has no 3-second minimum; the older plays metric (before an April 2025 cutover) excluded replays.
findings.note: Meta Media Insights API reference (per search snippet) defines views as total times played; replay inclusion and the April 21, 2025 cutover per Metricool help (help.metricool.com/instagram-metrics-ght51); Brandwatch notes the 3-second rule belonged to the deprecated metric. Seamless loops raise Instagram views.

findings.claim: Since March 31, 2025 YouTube counts a Shorts view each time a Short starts or replays, with no minimum watch time; the previous count is kept as engaged views, which still governs YPP eligibility and revenue.
findings.note: TechCrunch and others quote YouTube's support wording. Loops raise Shorts views but not engaged views.

findings.claim: YouTube Studio reports 'Viewed (vs. Swiped away)' for Shorts: the percentage of viewers who chose to view a Short versus swiped away. YouTube publishes no benchmark.
findings.note: Definition from YouTube Help (search snippet). Third-party targets of roughly 70-80% viewed are not YouTube guidance; compare against your own Shorts of similar length.

findings.claim: Facebook IQ (2016) reported people recall mobile feed content at a statistically significant rate after 0.25 s of exposure (Fors Marsh Group tests) and spend on average 1.7 s with a piece of content on mobile vs 2.5 s on desktop.
findings.note: Company research about its own platform; methodology not public. Supports a frame 1 that carries the promise visually before any word lands.

findings.claim: A 2015 Facebook-commissioned Nielsen study found even 3-second video views lift ad recall (47%), awareness (32%) and purchase intent (44%); a widely repeated secondary framing says up to 47% of campaign value lands in the first 3 s and 74% in the first 10 s.
findings.note: The two framings conflict; cite the recall-lift version. Ad research, not organic Reels.

findings.claim: TikTok's creative guide for auction ads says over 63% of the highest-CTR videos highlight their key message or product within the first 3 seconds.
findings.note: TikTok primary document (per search snippet). About ads, but the clearest platform statement that the proposition belongs in seconds 0-3.

findings.claim: TikTok Marketing Science research (Metrixlab, 2023, US/UK/GCC) reportedly found about half of an ad's impact is realized in the first 2 seconds and the first 6 seconds capture about 90% of cumulative ad-recall impact (about 80% for awareness).
findings.note: Secondary coverage; original TikTok document not seen. Blog figures like '71% decide within 3 seconds' had no primary source.

findings.claim: Curiosity is a feeling of deprivation triggered when attention is drawn to a specific gap in one's knowledge; a small amount of priming information increases it (information-gap theory).
findings.note: Loewenstein 1994, Psychological Bulletin. Peer-reviewed primary source cited from memory, not re-opened this session. Rule: name the gap precisely in the first 7 s and close it inside the reel.

findings.claim: Curiosity is highest at intermediate confidence (inverted U: people are most curious about answers they half-know), and higher curiosity predicts better later recall of the answer and engages reward circuitry.
findings.note: Kang et al. 2009, Psychological Science. Cited from memory. Pick topics GTA fans half-know (trailers, Vice City, the delays) and reveal what they don't.

findings.claim: In high-curiosity states people also remember unrelated information presented while they wait for the answer better.
findings.note: Gruber, Gelman & Ranganath 2014, Neuron. Cited from memory. Facts placed between hook and payoff (inside the open loop) are retained better.

findings.claim: In ~7,000 New York Times articles over three months, content evoking high-arousal emotions (awe, anger, anxiety) was more likely to be most-emailed and low-arousal sadness less; positive beat negative overall; practical utility, interest and surprise also predicted sharing; experiments confirmed causality.
findings.note: Berger & Milkman 2012, Journal of Marketing Research. Cited from memory. Send lever: one awe beat (cosmic-scale number) or anxiety beat (leak/theft stakes) plus one practical fact per reel.

findings.claim: Across Upworthy's randomized headline tests (~105,000 variants, ~370 million impressions), each additional negative word in an average-length headline raised click-through by 2.3%, while positive words lowered it.
findings.note: Robertson et al. 2023, Nature Human Behaviour. Cited from memory. Text headlines, not video: use one honest stakes word (burned, stolen, locked, nobody), not doom-bait.

findings.claim: Retrospective evaluations are dominated by the peak and the end of an experience, with duration largely neglected (peak-end rule); people even preferred a longer painful episode that ended less badly.
findings.note: Kahneman, Fredrickson, Schreiber & Redelmeier 1993, Psychological Science. Cited from memory. Likes and sends are decided at the end: best reveal and shot at 80-92%, end right after.

findings.claim: Information processed in relation to oneself is remembered better than information processed for meaning alone (self-reference effect).
findings.note: Rogers, Kuiper & Kirker 1977, JPSP. Cited from memory. The mechanism behind second-person hooks.

findings.claim: Forward-referencing phrases ('this', 'here is why') work as a lure in news headlines and are a defining clickbait feature.
findings.note: Blom & Hansen 2015, Journal of Pragmatics. Cited from memory. Use forward reference for the midpoint rehook but pay it off within ~5 s or it reads as bait.

findings.claim: People accelerate effort as a goal approaches (coffee-card customers bought faster near the free coffee), and illusory head-start progress speeds completion (goal-gradient effect).
findings.note: Kivetz, Urminsky & Zheng 2006, JMR. Cited from memory. Countdown numerals make progress to launch visible; expect engagement to rise into launch.

findings.claim: People derive utility from anticipating pleasant events and may prefer to delay them to savor the wait (a kiss from a movie star was valued most after a few days' delay).
findings.note: Loewenstein 1987, The Economic Journal. Cited from memory. Pre-launch content sells anticipation itself; that hook expires on launch day.

findings.claim: In a real-world study the median time for a repeated daily behavior to reach habit automaticity was 66 days (range 18-254).
findings.note: Lally et al. 2010, EJSP. Cited from memory. Applying it to audience viewing habits is our extrapolation (estimate): a 7-day countdown alone will not build a habit.

findings.claim: Faster speech rates increased persuasion and perceived speaker credibility in experiments.
findings.note: Miller, Maruyama, Beaber & Valone 1976, JPSP. Cited from memory. Supports the reference's ~185 wpm delivery; the claim that 180-190 wpm stays comfortably intelligible comes from accelerated-speech research not re-checked this session.

findings.claim: Adding a human-scale perspective sentence to large numbers in news text improved readers' recall, estimation and error detection.
findings.source_url: not verified this session (Barrio, Goldstein & Hofman, Improving Comprehension of Numbers in the News, CHI 2016)
findings.note: From memory; DOI not checked. Basis for re-expressing each big number twice.

findings.claim: The popular claim that open loops work via the Zeigarnik effect (better memory for unfinished tasks) rests on inconsistent replications; a recent meta-analysis reportedly found no robust memory advantage, only a tendency to resume interrupted tasks.
findings.note: Lean on the information-gap mechanism instead: open a specific gap, close it inside the reel, open tomorrow's gap at the end.

findings.claim: Since December 2017 Facebook has demoted posts that goad interactions: vote baiting, react baiting, share baiting, tag baiting and comment baiting.
findings.note: Meta newsroom post cited from memory (URL not re-opened). No equivalent public Instagram Reels rule found this session, so the risk of 'comment X' or 'send this to 10 people' CTAs on Instagram is unverified.

findings.claim: Reference reel anatomy from its 243-word transcript: 25 sentences averaging 9.7 words (~3.2 s); first big number at word ~28 (~9 s); rehook 'Here's the part you never see' starts at word 119 of 243 (~49%, ~39-40 s), followed by 2-7 word staccato lines; history/stakes at words 152-215 (~62-88%); payoff 'the noise turns into a city' at words 219-231 (~90-95%); sign-off in the last ~2-3 s; bookend 'guarding' to 'guard it well'; ~13 cuts = one visual every ~6.2 s.
findings.note: Our count from the transcript in the brief, assuming a uniform ~3 words/s; per-word timestamps not measured.

findings.claim: Reference reel engagement mix one day after posting: 22,289 likes vs 149 comments (about 150 likes per comment); the format earns approval and probably sends rather than discussion.
findings.note: Computed from counts in the brief (checked 2026-11-12). Views and shares not exposed, so sends are inferred.

findings.claim: The reference caption's arithmetic checks out: 2^128 = 3.4 x 10^38 keys; at 10^18 guesses/s that is 3.4 x 10^20 s = ~1.08 x 10^13 years, ~780 times a 13.8-billion-year universe, ~390 times for the average search.
findings.note: Our arithmetic. The narration's 212 GB, Denmark +50% traffic and code-in-box claims were not verified here.

findings.note: Matches Rockstar announcements known to mid-2026 and the reference's countdown, but not re-checked this session. May 26 to Nov 12, 2026 = 170 days (our arithmetic).

findings.claim: Rockstar's official GTA VI site lists six regions of Leonida: Vice City, Leonida Keys, Grassrivers, Port Gellhorn, Ambrosia and Mount Kalaga National Park.

findings.note: Well-established facts from memory; re-check before publishing. The Keys/Everglades parallels to Leonida regions are our reading and must be labeled so.

findings.note: From memory; current guidance not re-checked this session.

Transferable with your own labels.
